FitPulse - B2B
Wellbeing Dashboard

Case Study Product Designer

Note: Client and company names, along with the color palette, have been altered for confidentiality. The core UX process, decisions, and screens reflect a real B2B wellbeing dashboard project.

Overview

FitPulse is a B2B wellbeing platform used internally by client organizations to help HR teams and managers monitor employee wellbeing, engagement, and physical activity across departments. I worked on the UX for the platform's dashboard — designing the flows, structure, and key data views that HR and managers rely on daily.

Role

UI/UX Designer (dashboard structure, user flows, information architecture, desk research, AI assistant concept, contributed to visual design).

Duration - 6 months Platform - Web Dashboard

Problem

Client HR teams had access to raw wellbeing and activity data but no easy way to turn it into action. They needed a dashboard that could:

  • Surface org-wide wellbeing trends at a glance
  • Compare performance and risk across departments
  • Move HR from "here's the data" to "here's what to do about it"

Users

HR Managers — need org-wide visibility: wellbeing trends, department comparisons, burnout risk flags, and reporting.

Team Managers — need team-level insight: how their specific team is doing, participation in wellness activities, and where to intervene.

Process

I conducted desk research (competitor and best-practice analysis, AI-assisted synthesis of industry patterns) to understand how similar B2B wellbeing tools structured data for HR audiences. From there, I defined the dashboard's structure and built out wireframes and user flows for the core views, working closely with the co-founder and senior designer to shape the final direction. I also contributed to parts of the visual design as the product moved from wireframe to final UI.

Key questions I worked through:

  • How much data should surface at a glance vs. behind a click?
  • How do we make abstract wellbeing metrics (like "emotional state" or "sense of recognition") feel concrete and actionable?
  • How can the dashboard proactively guide HR toward next steps, rather than just displaying numbers?

Key Screens & Decisions

Wellbeing Dashboard (Overview)

The main view combines a global wellbeing score with a radar chart breaking it into dimensions — emotional state, motivation, work-life balance, team environment, and sense of recognition. A radar chart was chosen over a simple list of stats because it lets HR read the shape of wellbeing at a glance — is the dip concentrated in one area, or spread thin across several?

AI Assistant Integration

I proposed the idea of embedding a friendly AI assistant directly into the dashboard — a mascot-style presence (inspired by approachable, character-led assistants like Duolingo's) that would feel human and encouraging rather than clinical. The co-founder liked the direction, and after discussion with the co-founder and senior designer, it was developed into "Emi" — an assistant that surfaces proactive insights, such as flagging that a specific department's "rest & recovery" score is low, and suggesting concrete interventions (a wellness workshop, a digital disconnection policy). This shifted the dashboard from passive reporting to active guidance, reducing the analysis burden on HR teams who aren't data specialists.

Department & Burnout Insights

A breakdown of wellbeing status by department (High wellbeing / Stable / Signs of strain / High risk) lets HR quickly prioritize where to focus attention, rather than digging through department-by-department reports manually.

Activity Insights (Steps, Detox, Floors)

Supporting views track engagement with wellness activities — smartphone detox time, step counts, challenge participation — giving HR a fuller picture of how wellbeing initiatives translate into behavior change.

Outcome

The project was paused due to company funding issues before reaching full rollout. The wireframes, flows, and structure shown here reflect the UX work completed during the engagement.
